headline: Young people in China are raising bricks as pets

sources.title: 'Zero-energy companionship': bizarre hobby takes seed among China's stressed young adults (The Guardian)
年轻人"养砖头"须防健康隐患 (Young people who "raise bricks" should guard against health risks) (Xinhua, in Chinese, Sept 22, 2026)
China's Young Workers Are Raising Discarded Bricks as Pets (Trending on Weibo)

chunks.text: Young adults in China have {{picked up}} an unusual hobby. They "raise" [[ordinary]] bricks like pets. Owners spray a brick with water a few times a day. Then they wait for [[moss]], a soft green plant, to grow on it. The moss grows from [[spores]], tiny cells in the air that work like seeds. The trend has {{taken off}} online. Posts with one tag about it have more than 5 million views on a Chinese social media app.

verbs.correct: To start doing a new activity
verbs.wrong: To laugh at a new activity
verbs.why: Many retired people pick up painting as a hobby. My brother picks up a new sport every summer. Young adults in China have picked up the hobby of raising bricks.
Some songs take off after one funny video. A new snack sometimes takes off in just a few days. The brick trend has taken off online in China.

chunks.text: A brick's tiny holes {{soak up}} the water and keep it [[damp]]. If an owner forgets to water it, the moss goes [[dormant]], which means it rests. When the watering starts again, the green color {{comes back}}. Fans call them "brick babies." Many {{show off}} photos of their bricks as they change over a year. "No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick," one owner wrote.

verbs.correct: To absorb water like a sponge
verbs.why: A sponge soaks up water very fast. Dry soil soaks up the rain in minutes. A brick's tiny holes soak up the water and keep it damp.
The leaves on our tree come back every spring. My cat always comes back home at dinnertime. When the watering starts again, the green color comes back.

verbs.correct: To proudly let people see something
verbs.wrong: To sell something on the internet
verbs.why: She shows off her new shoes to her friends. He shows off photos of his garden online. Many brick owners show off photos of their bricks as they change.

chunks.text: For many owners, the small [[daily care]] {{pays off}}. One told Chinese media that it gives a [[sense of accomplishment]], like finishing a long project. Another owner wrote online that a brick has no goals to hit and never has to {{keep up with}} other people's bricks. Chinese commentators link the trend to the [[pressure]] young people feel. A hard [[job market]] {{stresses many young people out}}. Officially, nearly one in five people aged 16 to 24 who are not students have no job.

verbs.wrong: To take a very long time
verbs.why: Hard work usually pays off in the end. Saving a little money each week pays off over time. For many owners, the small daily care of a brick pays off.

verbs.correct: To do as well as other people
verbs.wrong: To give advice to other people
verbs.why: Some students study every night to keep up with their classmates. Small shops find it hard to keep up with big stores. Another owner wrote that a brick never has to keep up with other people's bricks.
Exams stress many students out. Long lines at the airport stress me out. A hard job market stresses many young people out in China.

chunks.text: Some young people are also {{giving up}} the race for top jobs. They choose "[[lying flat]]," a life with low [[effort]] and low stress. A brick costs almost nothing, and it helps some owners {{wind down}}. In September 2026, Chinese state media warned about [[mold]] on wet moss. Some owners have {{ended up}} with [[itchy eyes]] and [[runny noses]]. A [[retired]] moss expert suggests {{putting on}} [[disposable gloves]] and a mask.

verbs.why: Many players give up their dream of a pro career. Some people give up the search for a better job. Some young people in China are giving up the race for top jobs.

verbs.correct: To relax after a busy time
verbs.why: I read a book to wind down at night. Many people take a warm bath to wind down. Caring for a brick helps some owners wind down.

verbs.correct: To finally be in a situation
verbs.why: People who skip sleep often end up sick. Tourists without a map sometimes end up in the wrong town. Some brick owners have ended up with itchy eyes and runny noses.
I put on a warm coat when it is cold. Nurses put on gloves before they touch a patient. A retired moss expert suggests putting on disposable gloves and a mask.

mainIdea.s: Many young adults in China now care for plain bricks and wait for moss to grow. The cheap, easy hobby helps them relax in hard times, but Chinese media warn it can bring mold.
mainIdea.why: Young people have picked up brick raising as a cheap way to wind down. Chinese media also warn about mold and health problems.

mainIdea.s: Young people in China keep mossy bricks at home because doctors say the plants clean the air. Health officials hope that millions more will start the new hobby this winter.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Chinese commentators link the trend to stress and a hard job market. Chinese media actually warn that moss can bring mold and itchy eyes.

mainIdea.s: A building company in China has started selling green bricks covered in living moss for new apartments. It says the walls will keep homes cool and lower energy bills in summer.
mainIdea.why: This story is about young adults who raise ordinary bricks like pets. Many of them show off photos of their bricks online.

tf.s: If owners forget to water a brick, the moss dies and never returns.
tf.why: The moss only rests. When the watering starts again, the green color comes back.

tf.s: Many owners show off photos of their bricks online.
tf.why: They share pictures of how their bricks change over a year.

tf.s: A hard job market stresses many young people out in China.
tf.why: Officially, nearly one in five people aged 16 to 24 who are not students have no job.

tf.s: Chinese media say moss bricks are completely safe to keep at home.
tf.why: They warn about mold on wet moss, and some owners have ended up with itchy eyes and runny noses.

lines.text: Did you hear that young people in China are raising bricks as pets?
Bricks? Like the ones in a wall?
Yes. They spray them with water every day until moss grows on them.
It is. The brick's tiny holes {{soak up}} the water. And if you forget, the green {{comes back}} when you start again.
So you don't need a [[green thumb]].
Not at all. And the trend has really {{taken off}}. Posts about it have millions of views.
Why do people like it so much?
A hard job market {{stresses a lot of young people out}}. A brick gives them company with [[no strings attached]].
I get the appeal. There's no need to {{keep up with}} anyone.
Right. One owner said the daily care {{pays off}} with a real feeling of success.
Well, [[it's the little things]]. It probably helps them {{wind down}}, too.
Many {{show off}} photos of their bricks as they turn green.
Chinese media have warned about mold. Some owners have {{ended up}} with itchy eyes.
An expert says to {{put on}} gloves and a mask when you touch them.
Good. A little care gives you [[peace of mind]].
